new_en: That Kiddush be recited in the place of the meal. It contains 7 seifim: Kiddush is valid only in the place of the meal. Within one house, from corner to corner is considered one place. If one recited Kiddush intending to eat in this corner and then changed his mind to eat in another corner, even if it is a large hall, he need not recite Kiddush again. {Rama: And from the house to the sukkah is considered like from corner to corner. [Mordechai, chapter Arvei Pesachim]} And some say that anyone who sees his place, even from a house to a courtyard, need not recite Kiddush again. And some say that if one recited Kiddush in one place with the intention to eat in another place, it is effective (see above, beginning of siman 178), provided that the two places are in one house, for example from room to room or from the roof to the ground floor (and this is the primary view).
notes: Leftover fix: Rama restored in HE order; post-Rama Mechaber and non-hagah parentheticals restored outside Rama.

new_en: If two prayer services are before him, one Minchah and one Mussaf, for example he delayed Mussaf until 6 and a half seasonal hours, which is the time for Minchah, he must pray Minchah first and afterward Mussaf. {Rama: If, however, he prayed Mussaf first, he has fulfilled his obligation. [Beit Yosef in the name of Rashba]} And some say that this applies specifically when he presently needs to pray both, for example because he wishes to eat and may not eat until he has prayed Minchah; but if he does not presently need to pray Minchah, he may pray Mussaf first. {Rama: When the time of Minchah Ketanah has arrived, however, he should pray Minchah first. [Rosh in the name of the Yerushalmi]} And there is an authority who ruled that in a congregation one should not pray Minchah before Mussaf, lest people err.
notes: Leftover fix: congregation ruling restored after second Rama in HE order.

new_en: An item concerning which there is no concern of trapping or of having been detached from the ground, but which was merely brought from outside the techum: if a non-Jew brought it for himself, it is permitted even that same day. If he brought it for a Jew, it may be moved even by the one for whom it was brought, but eating it that same day is forbidden for the one for whom it was brought, and in the evening only after the amount of time required to perform the act has elapsed. {Rama: And some say that the night is not included in this calculation; rather, one must wait on the first weekday the amount of time required to perform the act. [Semak; Mordechai, end of chapter Kol Ketavei]} For others it is permitted that same day. And some say that for the one for whom it was brought it is permitted immediately in the evening. And the permission for a Jew to move it even when the non-Jew brought it for himself applies only within 4 amot, or within the city if it is surrounded by a wall, provided that it was enclosed for residential purposes, meaning that it was inhabited first and enclosed afterward. Ordinary towns are presumed to have been enclosed for residential purposes, whereas ordinary fortresses are not (see above, siman 401).
notes: Leftover fix: post-Rama Mechaber restored; siman 401 cross-ref kept as parenthetical (not hagah).

new_en: The laws of a courtyard smaller than 4 amot and of a drain. It contains 3 seifim: A courtyard smaller than 4 by 4 amot that adjoins the public domain — one may not pour water into it on Shabbos in the summer, because since it lacks 4 amot, the 2 se'ah of water that a person ordinarily uses each day will not be absorbed there, and it is as if he pours into the public domain. Therefore one must make a pit whose cavity holds 2 se'ah. {Rama: And any pit half an amah by half an amah with a height of three-fifths of an amah holds 2 se'ah. [Rambam]} This is so whether he makes it inside the courtyard or outside; but if he makes it outside, he must cover it with boards so that it will be a makom patur and the water will fall from his hand into a makom patur. Once he makes a pit, he may pour into it as much as he wishes. If it does not hold 2 se'ah, he may not pour into it at all. If the courtyard is 4 by 4, even if it is long and narrow, or in the rainy season even a courtyard of any size, one may pour into it as much as he wishes. A courtyard and an achsadrah — meaning a structure with 3 walls, and a fourth wall where a door is set that does not enclose at all except across the width of the house, and sometimes they make one amah of paneling on each side, so explained the Aruch, and a panel is a bit of straight, even wall — that neither alone has 4 amot combine to 4 amot to permit pouring into them. {Rama: And the same law applies to 2 galleries in front of 2 upper stories with a ceiling above them in which water can be absorbed: if they adjoin one another, they combine. [Beit Yosef in the name of Rabbeinu Yonatan]} When does this apply? Regarding a courtyard that adjoins the public domain. But if it adjoins a karmelit, even if it is very small, it does not need a pit even in the summer (see above, siman 377).
notes: Leftover fix: full HE translation; both Ramas in order; post-Rama karmelit clause restored.

new_en: Women and servants are exempt because it is a time-bound positive mitzvah. {Rama: Nevertheless, if they wish to wrap themselves in it and recite a blessing over it, they have permission to do so, as with other time-bound positive mitzvot. [Tosafos, Rosh, and Ran, chapter 2 of Rosh Hashana and chapter 1 of Kiddushin] However, it appears presumptuous; therefore they should not wear tzitzis, since it is not an obligation incumbent upon the person. [Agur, siman 27] Meaning: he is not obligated to purchase a tallis in order to become obligated in tzitzis. Below, in siman 19, he says that when one has a four-cornered garment and wears it.} A tumtum and an androgynos are obligated because of doubt and should wrap themselves without a blessing. [Meaning: a tumtum is one whose sex is unknown, and an androgynos has both male and female characteristics.] {Rama: And according to the custom that women recite blessings over time-bound positive mitzvot, they too should recite the blessing.} This gloss is Rama's own ruling.
notes: Leftover fix: both Ramas in HE order; dverei atzmo attribution after final Rama (post-Rama EN).

new_en: Raising and rubbing the hands when washing. It contains 10 seifim: One who washes must raise his hands (that is, the tips of his fingers) upward so that water will not flow beyond the joint and return and render the hands impure. {Rama: And the same law applies if he keeps them lowered from the beginning of the washing until the end, which is also valid; he must only be careful not first to raise the fingertips and then lower them, because then the water would flow beyond the joint and return and render the hands impure. [Beit Yosef in the name of Mahari ibn Chaviv]} This applies when one does not wash the entire hand up to the place where the hand joins the forearm; but if he washes up to there, he need not raise his hands (and some disagree about this). Likewise, if he poured a revi'it over both hands at once, since there is no impure water at all, he need not raise his hands. Likewise, one who immerses his hands need not raise his hands. (And some say that if one pours over his hands 3 times, he need not be careful about all of this, and the custom is to be lenient. [Agur in the name of Or Zarua and Hagahot Ashiri, chapter 25])
notes: Leftover fix: only true hagah as Rama; post-Rama Mechaber and 3-pour parenthetical restored outside Rama.

new_en: If one erred and did not mention Rosh Chodesh in Birkat HaMazon, whether by day or by night, he says, 'Blessed is He Who gave New Moons to His people Israel as a remembrance,' and does not conclude it with a blessing formula, provided that he remembered before beginning HaTov VeHaMeitiv. But if he did not remember until after beginning HaTov VeHaMeitiv, he does not return, because he is not obligated to eat bread in a manner that requires Birkat HaMazon. And Chol HaMoed has the same law as Rosh Chodesh. {Rama: And it is possible that nevertheless one should say it among the other HaRachaman passages, as explained above at the end of siman 187 regarding Al HaNissim. And perhaps there is a distinction, because Ya'aleh VeYavo contains Divine Names and one should not recite them in vain. So it appears to me, and this is the custom.} If Rosh Chodesh falls on Shabbos and he mentioned Shabbos but not Rosh Chodesh, and he did not remember until after beginning HaTov VeHaMeitiv, he does not return. And if he forgot Shabbos as well and remembered before beginning HaTov VeHaMeitiv, he combines Rosh Chodesh with Shabbos and says, 'Who gave Shabbosos for rest and New Moons for remembrance.' And if he already began HaTov VeHaMeitiv, he returns to the beginning of Birkat HaMazon and mentions both Shabbos and Rosh Chodesh. And there is an authority who says that if he forgot both Shabbos and Rosh Chodesh and remembered before beginning HaTov VeHaMeitiv, he says, 'Who gave Shabbosos for rest and New Moons for remembrance,' and concludes with the concluding formula for Shabbos, and does not conclude with that of Rosh Chodesh.
notes: Leftover fix: Rama restored mid-seif; post-Rama Shabbos/Rosh Chodesh clauses restored.

new_en: The law of embarking on a ship and traveling with a caravan on Shabbos. It contains 4 seifim: It is permitted to embark on a ship even on Friday if one is traveling for the purpose of a mitzvah, and he stipulates with him that he will rest, and if afterward he does not rest, it is of no consequence. But for an optional journey one may not embark within 3 days before Shabbos. {Rama: But more than 3 days beforehand it is permitted even on a ship that is drawn by animals, even where the water is less than 10 tefachim deep. [Maharik, shoresh 45] And this is so even where the Jew will afterward need to perform a melacha on Shabbos in order to direct the ship. [Rivash, siman 152]} And if it is a short journey, such as from Tyre to Sidon, between which there is only a one-day journey, it is permitted to embark on Friday morning because it is possible to arrive there before Shabbos. And in a place where the custom is not to embark at all on Friday, even for a short journey, one does not embark.
notes: Leftover fix: Rama restored mid-seif; short-journey and custom clauses restored after Rama.

new_en: It is forbidden on Friday to establish a meal and drinking feast that one is not accustomed to have on weekdays, even if it is an engagement meal, because of the honor of Shabbos, so that one will enter Shabbos with an appetite. And the entire day is included in the prohibition. {Rama: And a meal whose time falls on Friday, such as a circumcision or pidyon haben, is permitted as explained above, and this is the prevalent custom.} And to eat and drink without establishing a meal, even a meal of the sort one ordinarily eats on a weekday, it is permitted by the strict law to begin throughout the day; but it is a mitzvah to refrain from establishing a meal that one is accustomed to have on weekdays from the ninth hour onward.
notes: Leftover fix: Rama restored mid-seif; post-Rama eating-without-kevi'ah clause restored.

new_en: The laws of relinquishing domain for those who forgot to make an eruv. It contains 2 seifim: All the laws of relinquishing domain that apply to one who forgot and did not join the eruv in his courtyard likewise apply in an alleyway. Thus, if one courtyard forgot and did not participate in the shituf, it may relinquish its domain to the other residents of the alleyway, or they to it, even though they are many, because the residents of a courtyard are considered, relative to the alleyway, like a single individual in a courtyard. And all the laws governing Jews in a courtyard together with a non-Jew likewise apply in an alleyway or in a city: carrying is not prohibited in an alleyway or in a walled city until there are 2 courtyards of Jewish houses in the city; but one courtyard does not suffice, even if many Jewish houses open into it. And this applies when the city is enclosed by a wall for residential purposes; ordinary towns are enclosed for residential purposes, and ordinary fortresses are not enclosed for residential purposes. And when there are 2 courtyards of Jewish houses in the city, one must rent from each and every courtyard of non-Jews, and it is not sufficient to rent from the city official. {Rama: And some say this is specifically regarding bringing objects into and out of the non-Jew's domain; but for carrying in the alleyway one may rent from the official, since the roadway of the alleyway belongs to the official and he can remove all the non-Jews from there. [Rivash, siman 710]} When does this apply? Regarding an official who does not own the houses and also has no right at all to use the houses of the city's residents, even in wartime. But in a place where all the city's needs are carried out only through the official or his appointee, renting from that official or from his agent certainly helps, because he has the right to place his men and weapons in the residents' houses in wartime without their consent.
notes: Leftover fix: post-Rama Mechaber about which official may be rented from restored outside Rama.

new_en: Not to prepare on one Yom Tov for another. It contains 2 seifim: It is forbidden to bake, cook, or slaughter on Yom Tov for the needs of the next day, even if it is Shabbos or Yom Tov, and even on the 2 days of Rosh Hashana. But a woman may fill a pot with meat even though she needs only one piece. {Rama: And all the more so may one slaughter even though he needs only a kezayit. [Semak] And likewise she may cook many pots and eat a little from each. [Beit Yosef; Rabbeinu Yeruham; and a responsum of Rashba]} And this is specifically before eating; but after eating she may not cook and say that she will eat a kezayit from it, because that is a ruse. Nevertheless, if she transgressed and cooked [or slaughtered], it is permitted to eat it.
notes: Leftover fix: post-Rama Mechaber about before/after eating restored outside Rama.

new_en: The laws of the sukkah on the seventh day. It contains 1 seif: Even if one finished eating on the morning of the seventh day, he should not dismantle his sukkah; but from Minchah onward he removes the utensils from it and prepares the house for the honor of the final Yom Tov. And if he has nowhere to clear his utensils and wishes to eat in it on Shemini Atzeret, he must reduce in it a place of 4 by 4, to make a recognition that he is sitting in it not for the mitzvah of sukkah, so that it should not appear as though he is adding. {Rama: And if he wishes to eat in the sukkah after the festival, he need not reduce it, because it appears as adding only on Shemini Atzeret. [Minhagim]} And if he still needs to eat during the rest of the day, he must eat in the sukkah, because its mitzvah applies all 7 days. And in the Diaspora, where one must sit in it on Shemini Atzeret, when he finishes eating on the eighth day he takes down his utensils and clears them from it. And if he has nowhere to take down his utensils and wishes to eat in it on the ninth, he cannot reduce it because it is Yom Tov. What should he do for recognition? If it was small, such that it was forbidden to place a lamp in it on the other days, he places a lamp in it; and if it is large, such that it is permitted to place a lamp in it, he brings into it pots and dishes and the like, in order to recognize that it is invalid and that its mitzvah has already ended.
notes: Leftover fix: Rama restored mid-seif; post-Rama seventh-day and Diaspora clauses restored.

new_en: The order of the Torah reading on Chanukah. It contains 3 seifim: We read the offerings of the nesi'im in Parashat Nasso, three each day, and we begin with Birkat Kohanim (and some say we begin with 'On the day Moshe finished,' [Tur], and this is our custom). And that passage is read with a Kohen and a Levi, and a Yisrael reads the offering of the first day (and some say that the Kohen reads that entire passage through 'on the first day,' and the Levi and Yisrael read 'on the first day,' [Minhagim], and this is our custom). On the second day the Kohen reads from 'On the second day' through 'one young bull,' the Levi through 'On the third day,' and the Yisrael repeats and reads 'On the second day,' and in this manner each day. {Rama: And some say that the Yisrael reads the following day's portion, namely 'On the third day,' and so on each day, and this is our custom. [Hagahot Maimoniyot, chapter 13]} On the eighth day we begin with 'On the eighth day,' complete the entire section, and read the first portion of Beha'alotcha (and the custom is to conclude with 'So he made the menorah.' [Minhagim]).
notes: Leftover fix: only true hagah as Rama; eighth-day Mechaber and menorah minhag restored after Rama.

new_en: It is permitted to give one's garments to a non-Jewish launderer and hides to a tanner (meaning the craftsman who tans and prepares the hides) close to nightfall, if he fixed a price with him or the non-Jew does them as a favor, provided that he does not tell him to do it on Shabbos, and also that the non-Jew performs the melacha in his own house. {Rama: And if he did not fix a price, it is forbidden on Friday. And see above, siman 247, for there are those who disagree when he does it for free, that is, as a favor.} And if he sees him performing his melacha on Shabbos, if he was doing it as a favor he must tell him not to do it on Shabbos. {Rama: And this is so even if he gave them to him several days before Shabbos.}
notes: Leftover fix: two separate {Rama} glosses matching two hagah blocks.

new_en: A Jew may give money to a non-Jew to do business with it, and even though the non-Jew buys and sells with it on Shabbos, he shares with him all the profit equally, because this melacha is not one that was incumbent upon the Jew to perform, such that the non-Jew would be acting as his agent, and likewise the business is not recognizable as belonging to whom. {Rama: And this is specifically in such a case, where the non-Jew alone buys and sells with the money; but if each one does business on his day, and the Jew must do business corresponding to what the non-Jew did on Shabbos, it is forbidden. [Beit Yosef in the name of a Gaon] And regarding a Jew who has a pledge from a non-Jew, see below, siman 325, seifim 2 and 3.}
notes: Leftover fix: translate THIS cell 245:4 (not wrong id 245:2); Rama restored.

new_en: The laws of a kirah and an oven, regarding placing a pot upon them before Shabbos. It contains 5 seifim: A kirah is made like a large pot, with room on its opening above for 2 pots. If it was heated with olive refuse or with wood, it is forbidden before Shabbos to place a cooked dish upon it to remain there, unless the dish is fully cooked and further reduction is detrimental to it, so that there is no concern that one may stir the coals, or unless the food is completely raw and has not cooked at all, because when it is raw one puts it out of mind until the next day and it can cook throughout the night without stirring the coals. But if it has cooked somewhat and is not fully cooked, or even if it is fully cooked but further reduction improves it, we are concerned that one may stir the coals, and it is forbidden to leave it there unless the kirah was garuf, meaning that all the coals were removed, or katum, meaning that the coals were covered with ashes to reduce their heat. If he placed a raw piece into the pot, it is permitted as though the entire dish were raw, because by doing so he puts it out of mind. Even when the kirah is neither garuf nor katum, it is permitted to place a pot adjacent to it on the outside. If it was heated with straw or stubble, one may leave a pot upon it even if it is neither garuf nor katum. {Rama: If 2 kirahs adjoin one another with an earthenware wall between them, one being garuf and katum and the other not garuf and katum, it is permitted to leave food on the garuf and katum one even though it receives additional heat from the one that is not garuf and katum. [Gemara, chapter Kirah]} An oven, even if heated with straw or stubble, is forbidden even for placing a pot adjacent to it, even if it is garuf and katum. {Rama: All this applies while it is yad soledes bo. [Hagahot Mordechai]} All the more so is it forbidden to leave a pot inside it or on top of it. A kupach, which has room for 1 pot, has the law of a kirah if heated with straw or stubble, and the law of an oven if heated with olive refuse or wood (and our ovens have the law of a kirah. [Ran, beginning of chapter Kirah; Kol Bo; and so is implied by Rashi]). If one forgot and left a dish there, if it was fully cooked it is permitted even if further reduction improves it. If it had begun cooking but was not fully cooked, it is forbidden until after Shabbos. If he deliberately left it there in violation of the law, it is forbidden in both cases. {Rama: Until after Shabbos for the amount of time required for the act to have been done. [Hagahot Ashiri; Rambam, chapter 3] If a non-Jew returned them on Shabbos, the law is like one who forgot and left them there. [Hagahot Ashiri] If a Jew returned them, the law is like one who deliberately left them there. [Hagahot Mordechai] And if further reduction is detrimental to it, it is permitted, because he derived no benefit from the prohibition. [Beit Yosef; and see above at the beginning of siman 227]} And some say that whenever it has cooked to the degree of ma'achal ben Derusai — meaning the name of a person who would eat his food when it was not fully cooked — or it is fully cooked and further reduction improves it, it may be left on a kirah. {Rama: Or even on top of an oven. [Maggid Mishneh, chapter 3; Hagahot Mordechai; Maimoniyot, chapter 3; beginning of chapter Kirah in Beit Yosef]} This applies even if it was heated with olive refuse or wood and even if it is neither garuf nor katum. Garuf and katum, and heating with straw or stubble, were mentioned only where it had begun to cook but had not reached ma'achal ben Derusai; and likewise regarding if one removed the pot from upon it and wishes to return it upon it on Shabbos. And if one forgot and left a dish that had begun cooking but had not reached ma'achal ben Derusai, it is forbidden, and needless to say if he deliberately left it there. {Rama: And the custom is to be lenient in accordance with the latter view.} All of this regarding leaving applies when the pot sits on an iron stand or on stones and does not touch the coals; but insulating upon coals is forbidden according to all opinions. {Rama: And some say that even if the pot stands directly upon the fire, as long as it is uncovered on top it is not called insulation and is permitted, and this is the custom; only they are careful to detach it somewhat from the fire before Shabbos so that a Jew will be able to remove it from there. And if he did not detach it from the fire and finds it upon the fire on Shabbos, it should be removed by a non-Jew. And if there is no non-Jew, a Jew may remove it from there, and he should be careful to take it gently and not move the coals; and then even if he moves them slightly, an unintended act is permitted. [Mordechai, beginning of chapter Kirah; Hagahot Maimoniyot, chapter 7]}
notes: Leftover fix: replaced banned hand recoils with yad soledes bo; six Ramas matching six hagah; our-ovens kept as parenthetical.
